title: Beginner To Master | Chess Speedrun | Najdorf Sicilian | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We answer the king's pawn with c5 — the Sicilian, heading for the Najdorf.
We continue with d6.
White opens the centre with d4 — the Open Sicilian.
We capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight and we develop our knight to f6. After White's knight to c3 we'd have several roads — ...g6 for the Dragon, ...Nc6 for the Classical, ...e6, or ...e5.
White develops the knight to c3.
The Najdorf's signature move: a6, dear to every Sicilian player. Its first point is simple — it covers b5, keeping White's knight and bishop off that square.

White chooses the bishop to e2 — a very popular reply, and White's quietest. But "quiet" is relative: the position stays sharp. It's called quiet because here White castles short, whereas in the bishop-g5 and bishop-b3 systems White castles long and both sides storm opposite wings.
Najdorf players broadly split into two camps — the ...e6 players, heading for a Scheveningen structure, and the ...e5 players.
We play e5. To an outsider this looks bizarre — if it doesn't strike you as strange, you're missing something. ...e6 would give the Scheveningen; the ...e5 Najdorf is our choice.

White retreats the knight to b3. Now, why does ...e5 look like a blunder? It weakens the d6-pawn and, above all, the d5-square. This is exactly why the Najdorf isn't for beginners — you're breaking basic positional rules, and you only earn that right once you truly know them. There's no single reason ...e5 holds up; it's a web of them, and the first is the most basic: we get on with development.

We develop the bishop to e7 — the main move, readying quick castling; the c8-bishop may later fianchetto to b7. Here's the first strand of the web: we have a crowd of pieces to fight for the d5-square.

White castles. Concretely: our bishop can go to e6 and the f6-knight be backed up by its partner from d7 — two pieces directly and one indirectly guarding d5, so White can rarely plant a knight there and make it stick.

We castle. The second strand: we get counterplay on both wings, the ...b5 advance in particular offsetting the d5 weakness. Even so, the hole is real — a knight that lands on d5 and stays can decide the game, so it must be respected, never ignored.
The bishop-e2 Najdorf is a quiet but deep line — Karpov, one of history's great positional players, championed it for its balance of the tactical and the positional.

The ...e6 Scheveningen avoids weakening d5, but it carries real drawbacks: it hems in the light-squared bishop, the e6-pawn becomes a target for White's f4–f5 plan, and Black stays cramped, which makes a kingside attack hard to meet. Playing ...e5 instead makes it harder for White to attack at all.
It's the same reason many players avoid the French — you keep landing in these cramped structures.

A key idea for White here is the queen to d3, over-protecting e4 — that frees the c3-knight from guarding the pawn, so it can head for d5. Here, though, we can capture on d5, giving sharp opposite-wing play rather than letting White keep a dominant outpost.
White tries f4. It's playable, but without the bite it would carry if our pawn were back on e6 — here we can simply take on f4.
We capture, exf4.

White recaptures with the bishop on f4. Now a very typical picture: the d6-pawn looks weak, but just as bad bishops defend good pawns, bad pawns defend good squares — d6 underpins a knight bound for e5, where it sits like a rock. This capture on f4 followed by the knight to e5 is one of the oldest, most classical Najdorf ideas.
